name: Platform shoes for height (Bogart trick)

card.summary: Raised soles or blocks added to shoes, as film actors have used on set, to add a few inches of standing height.
card.aka: Platform shoes, shoe blocks, shoe lifts, elevator shoes
card.note: Height gain lasts only while worn; thick lifts affect balance and gait.

quick.overview:
The 'Bogart trick' refers to the practice of putting blocks or raised soles under an actor's shoes so he appears taller next to a co-star. Wikipedia reports that on Casablanca Humphrey Bogart had 3-inch blocks attached to his shoes in some scenes because Ingrid Bergman was taller.

The same idea is used by anyone who wants more standing height: a raised sole adds its thickness directly, visible in photos and in person. Platform shoes put the height in the sole, while elevator shoes hide it in a thickened insole.
quick.how: Options range from visible platform soles to shoes with a thickened internal heel lift. Film productions have also used blocks fixed to shoes or raised ground. Wearers pick shoe styles that suit the added height, and thicker lifts change how the foot sits and walks.
quick.risks: Taller lifts raise the heel and can alter balance and gait, and platform footwear fashions have in the past been associated with falls and injuries and safety warnings. Height gained is temporary, ending when the shoes come off.

lead: Platform shoes and shoe lifts raise the wearer's feet and so add standing height directly. The 'Bogart trick' takes its name from reports that Humphrey Bogart wore 3-inch blocks attached to his shoes in some scenes of Casablanca because co-star Ingrid Bergman was taller.[1]

People use the approach to look taller in photos, at work and on dates. Platform footwear has appeared in many eras: Vogue in 1937 wrote that the new cork-soled sandals added three inches to the length of the legs, platforms peaked in popularity in the early 1970s, and they returned in the 1990s with platform sneakers.[2] Elevator shoes, by contrast, hide a thickened insole under the heel so the lift is not visible.[3]
No clinical studies cover the use of platform shoes for height.

angle.text: A raised sole adds height equal to its thickness for as long as the shoes are worn. Users pick visible platforms or hidden insoles depending on how obvious they want the lift to be.

paras: Platform footwear appears across history, including Greek theatre, Roman buskins and Venetian chopines. Salvatore Ferragamo, André Perugia and Delman popularised platforms in the late 1930s, wartime leather rationing pushed designers to cork and wood, and Roger Vivier revived them in 1967.[2] Platforms peaked in the early 1970s and then fell from fashion after falls and injuries led to safety warnings.[2]
Bogart's blocks on Casablanca are the best-known example, and the practice of raising shorter leading men beside taller co-stars gave the technique its nickname.[1]

timeline.event: Vogue describes cork-soled sandals as adding three inches to the legs.[2]
